references.text: God took the man and placed him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it – a direct elaboration that God placed Adam in the garden.
God sends Adam out of the garden of Eden after the fall and sets cherubim to guard the way to the tree of life – the dramatic contrast to God originally placing humanity in the garden.
Lot sees the Jordan valley and compares it to the Lord's garden (the garden of Eden), showing that Eden was used as a standard for fertility and beauty.
Isaiah prophesies that the Lord will comfort Zion and make her wilderness like Eden and her desert like the Lord's garden – an eschatological restoration of paradise.
Ezekiel mentions Eden, God's garden, in connection with the king of Tyre – a significant reference to the garden of Eden as God's special place.
Ezekiel describes that the devastated land will become like the garden of Eden – a prophecy of restoration using the garden of Eden as an image of perfect blessing.
Joel describes that the land before the enemy is like the garden of Eden, but behind them a desolate wilderness – Eden is used as an image of fertility and abundance.
Revelation promises the one who overcomes to eat from the tree of life in God's paradise – an eschatological return to the garden of Eden and the tree of life that was there.
3:23 marks the end of the stay in the garden that began in 2:8, completing the cycle from creation to fall.
1:27 provides the theological basis (the image of God) for humanity who is placed in the garden in 2:8.
4:24 shows the final consequence of humanity's original placement in 2:8 by blocking the way back.
